target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society overall because it improves convenience, health, work, accessibility, and workplace safety.
objection: AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses, undermines critical thinking, hurts racial minorities by repeating and exacerbating racism, and poses dangerous privacy risks; because these are serious wide-ranging harms, AI is not good for society overall.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking by giving learners answers and explanations that replace independent reasoning.
objection: AI can strengthen critical thinking instead of weakening it because interactive learning support can provide explanations, examples, practice, and feedback that help students and adults evaluate information, detect errors, and improve reasoning.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms economic well-being through automation and displacement.
objection: AI can improve economic well-being by automating routine work, raising productivity, helping students and professionals be more effective, and supporting retraining for people transitioning to new tasks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI causes serious privacy and discrimination harms that remain even with safeguards.
objection: Privacy and fairness safeguards such as data minimization, access controls, encryption, auditing, and bias testing can substantially reduce the likelihood and impact of surveillance, profiling misuse, and discriminatory outputs.

target: AG1’s claim that AI safeguards can adequately prevent harms and that AI’s benefits outweigh its risks.
objection: Even if AI improves safety and accessibility, those benefits are not sufficient by themselves to make AI good overall, because serious harms can still coexist in other central welfare dimensions such as privacy, economic well-being, racial equality, and critical thinking.

target: AG1’s claim that AI safety and accessibility benefits outweigh or offset job displacement effects.
objection: AI-driven automation substitutes for human labor, reducing employment opportunities and wages for some workers; these displacement harms are broader than the subset of workers who gain safety benefits, so safety gains do not offset economic losses for most affected people.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits in everyday convenience, health, productivity, inclusion, and safety establish that AI is good overall if harms can be managed.
objection: Even substantial benefits in several welfare dimensions do not settle the issue because privacy, economic well-being, racial equality, and critical thinking are also central welfare dimensions, and AI’s harms in those areas can outweigh its benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that AI discrimination is mainly a governance issue that can be corrected through safeguards like human review, bias testing, and user challenge procedures.
objection: In high-stakes AI settings, decisions are often opaque and hard to contest; regulators and audits document persistent transparency and contestability gaps, and effective governance measures are too resource-intensive and technically difficult to sustain widely enough to stop discrimination from recurring.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s racial discrimination is inevitably persistent because decisions are opaque and unchallengeable.
objection: AI deployments can include human oversight, auditing, bias testing, documentation, and notice/appeal procedures, making outcomes more understandable and contestable so that discriminatory errors can be corrected rather than inevitably persisting.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can broadly solve discrimination in high-stakes AI.
objection: Meaningful oversight, bias auditing, and contestation require access to model behavior and data, plus sustained expert time; proprietary secrecy, cost, and speed pressures in real deployments make these safeguards impossible to implement broadly enough to materially reduce persistent discrimination at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that discriminatory harms in high-stakes AI will inevitably persist despite safeguards.
objection: If deployments include human oversight, auditing, and practical challenge/correction procedures, then discriminatory or erroneous outcomes can be corrected and need not persist at scale, so persistent racial-minority harm is not inevitable.

target: AG1’s claim that contestation and oversight can be implemented widely enough to prevent persistent discrimination.
objection: Those safeguards require notice, explanation, access to relevant data/model behavior, and ongoing staffing and compliance; in typical competitive real-world deployments, secrecy, cost, and fragmented oversight prevent them from being implemented at the scale needed to materially reduce persistent discriminatory harms.

target: AG2’s claim that high-stakes AI generally cannot be made understandable or contestable enough to avoid persistent discrimination.
objection: Lack of understandability and contestability is a governance issue, not an inevitable property of AI; with human review, auditing, documentation, and appeal procedures, affected people can have meaningful routes to challenge outcomes and discriminatory errors can be corrected.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can broadly satisfy accountability and contestation requirements in high-stakes uses.
objection: In typical high-stakes deployments, robust accountability mechanisms are not implemented with enough breadth and depth because of cost, time, proprietary secrecy, and fragmented oversight, so discriminatory errors often remain uncorrected and harms persist.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s worst discriminatory harms are inherent and decisive against AI being good overall.
objection: AI can still be judged good for society overall if it delivers substantial welfare benefits and its worst discriminatory harms are materially reduced rather than inevitably persistent through safeguards like bias testing, human oversight, and appeal procedures.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards against discrimination can be broadly implemented in typical high-stakes AI uses.
objection: Effective safeguards require continuous access to relevant data and model behavior, actionable understanding of outputs, and ongoing revalidation; because proprietary pipelines, data drift, and cost/operational burdens make these requirements hard to meet continuously and broadly, the safeguards cannot be implemented widely enough to materially reduce persistent discriminatory harms.
